item.text: {"text":"Strong in-sample margins against uniform negatives provide weak evidence of useful full-catalog ranking. Sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; increasing repetitions does not eliminate this bias ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). A RecSys 2025 study assesses sampling through resolution, fidelity to full evaluation, robustness, and recovery of model rankings ([On the Reliability of Sampling Strategies](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086)). Sequential-recommendation experiments from 2024 also show that aggregate scores conceal head/mid/tail disparities: random negative sampling favored head items, while popularity-based sampling improved balance with potential aggregate-performance costs ([Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276)).\n\nPractical implication for this task: use fixed training-prefix/next-item probes with unique uniform, target-popularity-matched, and title/description lexical-hard candidates. Treat lexical hardness as a proposed stress test, not established irrelevance; hard unobserved items may be false negatives ([negative-sampling survey](https://doi.org/10.1145/3793855)). Report target-rank distributions, pairwise win rates, and margins separately for each candidate pool. On a bounded, fixed user subset, compare sampled target ranks with full-catalog ranks and top-10 membership; measure checkpoint-order agreement and failure concentration by prefix length and training-only item-frequency bands in each of the four datasets. These are diagnostic proposals, not reported experimental findings. Training-position success measures fit and cannot establish generalization; prefix-only inputs prevent future-context leakage but do not undo parameter exposure to trained targets. Keep these audits separate from the unchanged host macro validation HR@10 used for selection."}
